misconceptions.name: Wrong logical relation
misconceptions.description: The student misdiagnoses the logical relationship between the two sentences and selects a transition from the wrong family — for example contrast ('however') where the link is cause-effect ('therefore'), or addition ('moreover') where it is contrast.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a transition naming a different logical family than the one actually connecting the two sentences (e.g. a contrast transition for a cause-effect pair).
misconceptions.remediationNote: Have the student name the relationship in one word (contrast, cause, example, addition, concession, sequence) before looking at the choices, then pick the transition that names exactly that relation.

misconceptions.name: Right family, wrong polarity
misconceptions.description: The student picks a transition from the correct logical family but with reversed direction, treating a parallel case as opposed (or vice versa) — e.g. 'conversely' for a case that is actually parallel.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a same-family transition with inverted polarity relative to the true relationship (e.g. 'conversely' where the sentences are parallel, not opposed).
misconceptions.remediationNote: Drill minimal pairs within a family (similarly/conversely, indeed/even so) and train the habit of asking whether sentence 2 continues or reverses sentence 1's direction.

misconceptions.name: Connector fits sentence 2 alone, not the pair
misconceptions.description: The student evaluates the transition against the second sentence's internal logic rather than the link between the sentences, choosing a connector that coheres within sentence 2 but misdescribes the sentence-to-sentence relationship.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a connector that coheres with sentence 2's internal content while misdescribing the link between sentence 1 and sentence 2.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Teach students to read the pair as a unit: ask 'what does sentence 2 do to sentence 1?' before judging any connector, since a transition's job is to bridge the sentences, not to decorate the second one.

misconceptions.name: False exemplification
misconceptions.description: The student assumes sentence 2 illustrates sentence 1 and selects 'for example' even when sentence 2 is not an instance of a general claim — or rejects exemplification when sentence 2 genuinely is such an instance.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an exemplification/illustration transition ('for example', 'for instance') where sentence 2 is not an instance of sentence 1's general claim.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Test exemplification explicitly: can sentence 2 be rewritten as 'an instance of <sentence 1's claim>'? If not, 'for example' is wrong no matter how related the topics feel.

misconceptions.name: Redundant or off-register connector
misconceptions.description: The student overlooks that a connector duplicates meaning already expressed in the sentences or clashes tonally with the passage's register.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a connector that duplicates meaning already present in the sentences or is tonally wrong for the passage.
misconceptions.remediationNote: After inserting a candidate, read the pair aloud and check for doubled logic (a cause already signaled in the wording) and for register consistency with the surrounding prose.

misconceptions.name: Comma splice
misconceptions.description: The student believes a comma alone can join two independent clauses, producing a comma splice.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose the option joining two independent clauses with a comma alone.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Teach the independent-clause test: if both sides of the boundary can stand alone as sentences, a comma needs a coordinating conjunction, or the boundary must be a semicolon or period.

misconceptions.name: Semicolon before an incomplete element
misconceptions.description: The student treats the semicolon as a generic strong pause, placing it before a dependent clause, a phrase, or an otherwise incomplete second element.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a semicolon where the element before or after it is not an independent clause.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Semicolons join equals: both sides must be independent clauses. If either side is fragmentary, the boundary needs a comma, colon, or no punctuation as the governing rule dictates.

misconceptions.name: Missing required punctuation
misconceptions.description: The student fails to set off a parenthetical, appositive, or introductory element, or leaves a paired comma or dash unclosed.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose the option with no punctuation (or only one mark of a required pair) where a supplement or introductory element must be set off.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Teach the deletion test: if an element can be removed without breaking the core sentence, it must be enclosed by a matched pair of punctuation marks — two commas, two dashes, or parentheses.

misconceptions.name: Punctuation splitting inseparable elements
misconceptions.description: The student inserts a boundary where none belongs — between subject and verb, inside a restrictive clause, or before 'because'.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose punctuation that splits elements that must stay together (subject from verb, within a restrictive clause, before 'because').
misconceptions.remediationNote: Drill the rule that a single comma never separates a subject from its verb or opens a restrictive modifier; punctuation follows syntactic structure, not pauses in speech.

misconceptions.name: Connector punctuation violation
misconceptions.description: The student picks a connector whose punctuation requirements the choice violates — e.g. using the conjunctive adverb 'however' with the punctuation licensed for the coordinating conjunction 'but'.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a conjunctive adverb punctuated like a coordinating conjunction (or vice versa), e.g. 'however' used like 'but'.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Contrast the two connector classes explicitly: 'but' takes a comma before it and nothing after; 'however' between independent clauses takes a semicolon before and a comma after.

misconceptions.name: Supporting detail inflated to main idea
misconceptions.description: The student mistakes a true subordinate point or example for the passage's central claim.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option presenting a true supporting detail as the main idea.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Ask: 'would the other sentences support this one, or does this one support them?' The main idea is the statement everything else in the passage serves.

misconceptions.name: Claim extended beyond its stated scope
misconceptions.description: The student accepts a broader version of the passage's claim — a wider population, stronger certainty, or larger scope than the text states.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option that extends the passage's claim beyond its stated scope or population.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Underline the passage's qualifiers (some, often, in this study) and require every word of the chosen option to be licensed by the text.

misconceptions.name: Stated relationship reversed
misconceptions.description: The student inverts a relationship the passage asserts — cause and effect swapped, or a comparison flipped ('more' read as 'fewer').
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option that swaps cause and effect or flips a comparison stated in the passage.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Sketch the passage's key relationship as an arrow (A -> B) before reading the options, and eliminate any option whose arrow points the other way.

misconceptions.name: Plausible but unsupported by the text
misconceptions.description: The student picks a statement that is true or plausible in the real world but that the passage never asserts.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option relying on outside knowledge that the passage never states.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Enforce a text-only rule: for each option, point to the exact lines that support it. If no lines exist, it cannot be the answer no matter how true it sounds.

misconceptions.name: Belief or finding assigned to the wrong source
misconceptions.description: The student attributes a belief, finding, or position to the wrong person, group, or time period named in the passage.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option assigning a belief or finding to the wrong person, group, or time period named in the passage.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Build a quick cast list while reading — who believes or found what — and check every attribution in the options against it.

misconceptions.name: Wrong cell of the table
misconceptions.description: The student reads the wrong row, column, or category when extracting data from the table or graph.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option citing data from the wrong row or column, or with categories swapped.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Trace the axes and labels physically before reading any values, and restate in words what the cited cell actually measures before matching it to the claim.

misconceptions.name: Accurate data, wrong job
misconceptions.description: The student selects a factually accurate statement about the data that does not bear on the claim it is supposed to support.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option whose numbers are accurate but irrelevant to the claim being supported.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Paraphrase the claim first, then ask of each option: 'if this is true, does the claim get more believable?' Accuracy is necessary but never sufficient.

misconceptions.name: Trend or comparison reported backwards
misconceptions.description: The student reports an increase as a decrease, or the higher value as the lower, reversing the direction of what the data show.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option reporting an increase as a decrease or the higher value as the lower.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Convert chart language into plain comparisons ('X rose, Y fell') and check each option against that plain statement before choosing.

misconceptions.name: Unit or scale confusion
misconceptions.description: The student ignores whether figures are percentages or counts, per-capita or totals, or otherwise misreads the scale of the data.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option that confuses percentages with counts, or per-capita figures with totals.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Always read the units in the axis, legend, or title first, and translate every cited figure into 'units of what, out of what' before comparing.

misconceptions.name: Whole-group figure applied to a subgroup
misconceptions.description: The student cites an overall figure when the claim concerns a subgroup, or a subgroup figure when the claim concerns the whole.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option citing an aggregate figure where the claim concerns a subgroup (or vice versa).
misconceptions.remediationNote: Match the scope of the data to the scope of the claim word by word — if the claim says 'among urban respondents', the evidence must be about urban respondents.

misconceptions.name: Evidence supports a nearby but different claim
misconceptions.description: The student selects a finding on the right topic that actually supports a different mechanism or conclusion than the claim stated in the stem.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a finding on the right topic that supports an adjacent claim, not the one the stem states.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Restate the exact claim — its mechanism, not just its topic — and require the evidence to make that specific mechanism more likely.

misconceptions.name: Evidence too weak to discriminate
misconceptions.description: The student accepts a finding that is consistent with the claim but equally consistent with rival explanations, so it does not count as support.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a finding that is consistent with the claim but does not discriminate between it and rival explanations.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Ask: 'would this finding also be true if the rival explanation were correct?' If yes, it is not supporting evidence for this claim.

misconceptions.name: Weakening evidence dressed as support
misconceptions.description: The student is swayed by supportive wording and misses that the finding actually weakens or complicates the claim.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a finding that actually weakens or complicates the claim, dressed in supportive wording.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Strip the rhetoric: state what the finding shows in neutral terms, then check its direction against the claim before trusting supportive phrasing.

misconceptions.name: Claim restated as its own evidence
misconceptions.description: The student accepts a paraphrase of the claim itself as if it were independent evidence for it.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option that restates the claim rather than providing independent evidence for it.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Evidence must add something the claim doesn't already say — an observation, result, or quotation that could exist even if the claim were false.

misconceptions.name: Evidence about the wrong population or variable
misconceptions.description: The student picks a finding about a different population, time period, or variable than the one the claim names.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a finding about the wrong population, time period, or variable relative to the claim.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Circle the claim's scope terms (who, when, what is measured) and eliminate any finding whose scope terms differ.

misconceptions.name: Positions attributed to the wrong text
misconceptions.description: The student attributes Text 1's position to Text 2, or vice versa.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option assigning one text's stance to the other text.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Summarize each text's position in a single labeled sentence ('Text 1: ...', 'Text 2: ...') before reading any options.

misconceptions.name: Relationship between the texts mislabeled
misconceptions.description: The student mislabels how the texts relate — claiming direct refutation where Text 2 merely complicates, or agreement where the texts address different questions.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option mislabeling the inter-text relationship (refutation vs complication, or agreement across different questions).
misconceptions.remediationNote: First decide whether the texts answer the same question, then whether Text 2 agrees, complicates, or contradicts — use graduated labels rather than an agree/disagree binary.

misconceptions.name: Response engages the wrong detail
misconceptions.description: The student selects a response that engages a detail of Text 1 other than the one the stem asks about.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option whose response engages a detail of Text 1 other than the one the stem targets.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Underline the specific claim or detail named in the stem and check that the chosen response engages exactly that element.

misconceptions.name: Position neither text supports
misconceptions.description: The student invents a stance for an author that neither text gives any basis to hold.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option attributing a position to an author with no basis in either text.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Every attributed view must be traceable to a specific line; if the author never commits to it, the option is fabrication.

misconceptions.name: Partial difference read as wholesale rejection
misconceptions.description: The student inflates a partial or conditional disagreement between the texts into total rejection.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option portraying a partial or conditional difference as wholesale rejection.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Calibrate strength words — 'challenges entirely' vs 'qualifies' — and match the option's strength to the text's actual strength.

misconceptions.name: Verb form inconsistent with time frame
misconceptions.description: The student picks a tense or aspect inconsistent with the sentence's time markers or the sequence of events.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a verb form inconsistent with the sentence's time markers or sequence of events.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Locate every time marker (by then, since 2010, next year) and sequence the events on a mental timeline before choosing the verb form.

misconceptions.name: Agreement with a decoy noun
misconceptions.description: The student makes a verb or pronoun agree with a nearby noun that is not its true subject or antecedent — misled by an intervening prepositional phrase, inverted order, or 'each/everyone' singulars.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a form agreeing with a nearby decoy noun rather than the true subject or antecedent.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Strip intervening phrases and locate the grammatical subject; remember that 'each', 'everyone', and inverted word order hide singular subjects.

misconceptions.name: Non-finite form where a finite verb is required
misconceptions.description: The student uses a participle or infinitive where a finite verb is required (or vice versa), producing a fragment or a dangling modifier.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a participle or infinitive where the sentence requires a finite verb (or vice versa), creating a fragment or dangling modifier.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Check that every clause contains a conjugated verb, and that any introductory participle logically attaches to the subject that follows it.

misconceptions.name: Pronoun case or number error
misconceptions.description: The student picks a pronoun in the wrong case or number, or confuses a possessive with a contraction ('its/it's', 'their/they're').
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a pronoun in the wrong case or number, or a possessive/contraction mix-up ('its/it's', 'their/they're').
misconceptions.remediationNote: Substitute the pronoun with the noun it replaces to hear the case, and expand contractions ('it's' = 'it is') to test them in the sentence.

misconceptions.name: Broken parallelism or illogical comparison
misconceptions.description: The student picks a form that breaks a parallel series or renders a comparison illogical ('more than any' vs 'more than any other').
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a form that breaks a parallel series or makes a comparison illogical.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Line up the items in a series and confirm each has the same grammatical form; in comparisons, check that like is compared with like.

misconceptions.name: Premise paraphrased instead of conclusion drawn
misconceptions.description: The student selects a choice that paraphrases a single premise instead of drawing a conclusion from the premises taken together.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option that paraphrases one premise rather than drawing a conclusion from the premises together.
misconceptions.remediationNote: The answer to an inference question must say something the passage doesn't state outright — ask 'is this new, or just repeated?'

misconceptions.name: Conclusion stronger than the premises license
misconceptions.description: The student accepts a conclusion that is stronger, broader, or more certain than the premises warrant ('always', 'proves', 'the only').
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a conclusion worded more strongly or broadly than the premises license.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Prefer the weakest defensible option, and flag absolute words — check whether the premises truly rule out every alternative.

misconceptions.name: Conclusion incompatible with a premise
misconceptions.description: The student overlooks that the chosen option is quietly incompatible with one stated premise.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option that contradicts a stated premise.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Test each option against every premise, not just the overall gist — one contradiction disqualifies it.

misconceptions.name: Real-world plausible but ungrounded
misconceptions.description: The student chooses a conclusion that sounds true in the real world but is not grounded in the passage.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a conclusion that is real-world plausible but not grounded in the passage.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Reason only from the given premises — pretend you know nothing about the topic outside the passage.

misconceptions.name: Conditional or correlation reversed
misconceptions.description: The student reverses the direction of a conditional or correlation the premises establish (treating 'if A then B' as 'if B then A').
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a conclusion that reverses the conditional or correlation the premises establish.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Restate the premise as an arrow and verify the conclusion's arrow points the same way; a correlation never licenses a reversed causal claim.

misconceptions.name: Accurate notes, wrong goal
misconceptions.description: The student picks a sentence that uses accurate notes but does not serve the stated rhetorical goal.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a sentence whose notes are accurate but which does not serve the stated goal.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Read the goal first and treat it as the question; a sentence can be factually perfect and still wrong if it doesn't do the requested job.

misconceptions.name: Nearby goal accomplished instead
misconceptions.description: The student picks a sentence that accomplishes a nearby but different goal — defining a term when the goal was to emphasize its influence, or narrating when the goal was to compare.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a sentence accomplishing a nearby but different goal than the stated one.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Classify the goal by its verb — emphasize, compare, introduce, illustrate — and check that the chosen sentence performs that exact rhetorical act.

misconceptions.name: Note subtly misstated
misconceptions.description: The student overlooks a small factual corruption in the sentence — a wrong date, a swapped attribution, or an inflated figure.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a sentence that subtly misstates a note (wrong date, swapped attribution, inflated figure).
misconceptions.remediationNote: Verify every fact in the chosen sentence against the notes one by one; a single corrupted detail disqualifies it.

misconceptions.name: Comparative goal, non-comparative sentence
misconceptions.description: When the goal asks for a comparison or contrast, the student accepts a sentence that merely lists facts side by side without making the comparative move.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a sentence that lists facts side by side where the goal requires a comparison or contrast.
misconceptions.remediationNote: A comparison needs comparative language ('whereas', 'unlike', 'more than') — a list of facts about both subjects is not a comparison.

misconceptions.name: Decisive note left out
misconceptions.description: The student accepts a sentence that addresses the goal but leaves out the single most decisive note, making it less effective than the key.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a sentence that addresses the goal but omits the most decisive note.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Rank the notes by relevance to the goal before reading the choices; the best sentence will use the top-ranked note.

misconceptions.name: What it says mistaken for what it does
misconceptions.description: The student accurately summarizes what a sentence says but misdescribes its rhetorical function in the passage.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option that accurately summarizes content but misdescribes the sentence's role.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Answer function questions with a verb, not a summary — ask 'what job does this sentence do for the argument?' (introduce, qualify, exemplify, concede).

misconceptions.name: Rhetorical roles swapped
misconceptions.description: The student describes evidence as the claim it supports, or a concession as the main assertion.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option describing evidence as the claim it supports, or a concession as the main assertion.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Map the passage's roles — which sentence asserts, which supports, which concedes — and assign each a label before reading the options.

misconceptions.name: Stronger move than the text makes
misconceptions.description: The student names a stronger rhetorical move than the text performs ('refutes' where the text merely 'qualifies'; 'proves' where it 'suggests').
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option naming a stronger rhetorical move than the text performs ('refutes' vs 'qualifies', 'proves' vs 'suggests').
misconceptions.remediationNote: Keep a graduated scale of strength verbs (suggests < argues < demonstrates < proves) and match the verb to the text's actual force.

misconceptions.name: Function of a different sentence
misconceptions.description: The student selects an accurate description of the function of a different sentence in the passage.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option describing the function of a different sentence than the one the stem asks about.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Locate the exact sentence named in the stem and test each option's description against that sentence alone.

misconceptions.name: Wrong architecture named
misconceptions.description: The student names a recognizable structure (chronology, problem-solution, compare-contrast) that fits a different passage shape than the actual one.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose an option naming a structure (chronology, problem-solution, compare-contrast) that does not match the passage's organization.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Outline the passage in two or three beats (e.g. claim -> objection -> reply) and match the option's architecture to that outline.

misconceptions.name: Right register, wrong meaning
misconceptions.description: The student is swayed by a word's matching formality and misses that its sense does not fit the context.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a word of matching formality whose sense does not fit the context.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Ignore tone first: paraphrase what the blank must mean in plain words, then find the choice that means exactly that.

misconceptions.name: Wrong sense of a polysemous word
misconceptions.description: The student selects a polysemous word whose tempting secondary meaning fails in context — or rejects the correct word because only its commonest sense comes to mind.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a polysemous word whose required sense fails in context (a secondary meaning tempts but does not fit).
misconceptions.remediationNote: Test each candidate's relevant dictionary sense in the sentence, not just its most familiar one — the SAT frequently tests secondary senses.

misconceptions.name: Near-synonym that doesn't collocate
misconceptions.description: The student picks a word close in meaning that does not combine naturally with the surrounding words (e.g. 'performed a mistake').
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a near-synonym that does not collocate naturally with the surrounding words.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Read the phrase aloud with each candidate; idiomatic English constrains which near-synonyms combine ('made a mistake', not 'performed a mistake').

misconceptions.name: Fits one clue, contradicts another
misconceptions.description: The student anchors on one clause's clue and misses that the chosen word contradicts another part of the sentence.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a word that satisfies one clause's clue while contradicting another.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Collect all the clues in the sentence — the blank must satisfy every one of them simultaneously.

misconceptions.name: Topic-associated but wrong for the slot
misconceptions.description: The student picks a word associated with the passage's topic even though it does not fit the blank's specific role in the sentence.
misconceptions.detectionSignal: Chose a word associated with the passage's topic but not with the blank's specific slot.
misconceptions.remediationNote: Topic relevance is a trap: the blank needs a word that fits the sentence's logic, not one that merely belongs to the subject area.
